```{r}
#| label: load-data

# Small tidy files produced by R/02_clean_data.R live in data/
# Where the people who live in each municipality go to work, 2021 census. Three
# rows per municipality, one per destination.
commuting <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "commuting.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# The share of workers who worked at home, 2016 and 2021 censuses: one row per
# district per year, plus the Region's own two rows. Built by 02_clean_data.R
# from tables 98-400-X2016321 (2016) and 98-10-0456 (2021).
work_at_home <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "work_at_home.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

# The share of the Region's workers who worked at home in each industry, 2016
# and 2021 censuses: one row per NAICS sector per year. Built by 02_clean_data.R
# from data table 98-400-X2016321 (2016) and table 98-10-0456 (2021).
work_at_home_industry <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "work_at_home_industry.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

# The Region's share in each year, ready to drop into a sentence with
# `r home_region_2016` and `r home_region_2021` (they print as "6.8%" and
# "29.0%"). The 2021 figure's 95% interval is a fraction of a point.
home_region <- work_at_home |>
  filter(district == cwr_region) |>
  mutate(label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent))
home_region_2016 <- home_region |> filter(year == 2016) |> pull(label)
home_region_2021 <- home_region |> filter(year == 2021) |> pull(label)
```

## No place like home

<!-- One or two paragraphs, then one chart. -->

::: panel-tabset
### Ranked

```{r}
#| label: work-at-home-2016
#| output: asis

# The 2016 shares on their own, ranked: one blue bar per district, each
# carrying its own number. The two tabs draw exactly the same chart; the only
# difference is the colour of the district names, white on this tab and the
# theme's own grey on the next, so the names are invisible here while still
# taking up their room. That keeps the bars in the same place on both tabs, so
# clicking between them only brings the names in. work_at_home is read in the
# load-data chunk; the Region's own row is left out, because the chart is by
# district.
home_2016 <- work_at_home |>
  filter(year == 2016, district != cwr_region)

# Roughly how many characters fit across the panel at this font size, read off
# a render; it decides whether a bar is long enough to hold its own label.
# (The destinations chart further down uses the same figure for the same job.)
panel_chars_home <- 40

home_2016 <- home_2016 |>
  mutate(
    # reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal chart draws the first level at
    # the bottom, so the district where most people worked at home ends up on top
    district = fct_reorder(district, percent),
    share_label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent),
    # Whether a bar can hold its own label
    inside = percent >= (nchar(share_label) + 1.5) * (max(percent) * 1.05 / panel_chars_home)
  )

# Built once and called by both tabs, which add their own titles.
# `show_names` is the whole difference between them.
home_2016_bars <- function(show_names) {
  ggplot(home_2016, aes(x = percent, y = district)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7, fill = dodgerblue) +
    # The baseline the bars grow from, stopping just past the end bars
    annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = nrow(home_2016) + 0.5,
             colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
    # White inside a bar that can hold its label, black just past one that cannot
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = share_label,
        hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
        colour = if_else(inside, "white", "black")
      ),
      size = label_size * 0.8
    ) +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    # Room on the right for a label that sits outside its bar
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
    # The house short form of a long district name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = cwr_short_name) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      axis.line.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
    ) +
    # The names in white on the first tab: drawn, measured and laid out as
    # usual, but the same colour as the page, so nothing moves when they appear
    (if (show_names) NULL else theme(axis.text.y.left = element_markdown(colour = "white")))
}

# The rows of an alt text, read top to bottom in the order the bars are drawn
home_2016_lines <- home_2016 |>
  arrange(desc(percent)) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(district, " ", share_label)) |>
  pull(line)

# ---- This tab ------------------------------------------------------------
p <- home_2016_bars(show_names = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of employed people who worked at home in 2016, by district",  # working title, descriptive only
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-400-X2016321",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        # The 2016 tables publish no interval for any count, so none can be
        # worked out for these shares (rule 9b)
        "No confidence intervals are published for these figures; shares close together may differ only by sampling error"
      )
    )
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-work-at-home-2016",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars ranking the Region's seven districts by the share of ",
    "employed people who worked at home in 2016, with the district names left ",
    "off. The shares, longest bar first: ",
    paste(
      home_2016 |> arrange(desc(percent)) |> pull(share_label),
      collapse = ", "
    ), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: work-at-home
#| output: asis

# The share of each district's workers who worked at home, in the 2016 and 2021
# censuses: two dots per row, 2016 in silver and 2021 in blue. work_at_home is
# read in the load-data chunk.
#
# The ggdumbbell template (the cwr-charts skill), with the year dots named on
# the top row instead of in its legend, and no highlighted row. The Region's
# own rows are left out: the chart is by district.
plot_data <- work_at_home |>
  filter(year %in% c(2016, 2021), district != cwr_region) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = district,
    names_from = year,
    values_from = percent
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Ordered on the 2021 share: reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal
    # chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the district with the most
    # people working at home ends up on top
    district = reorder(district, `2021`),
    # No row is highlighted; cwr_short_name() gives the house short form of a
    # long district name
    y_label = cwr_short_name(as.character(district))
  )

# Pre-compute labels to avoid data masking issue in scale_y_discrete
y_labels <- plot_data |> select(district, y_label) |> deframe()

# The right end of the background segments and of the x axis: just past the
# largest share, rounded up to the next 5
max_x <- ceiling(max(plot_data$`2021`) / 5) * 5

# The top row's two dots are named with their year instead of the template's
# legend: above the joining line and beside each dot, on the side facing the
# other dot - 2016 to its right, 2021 to its left. hjust sets which side of its
# anchor the text sits on (0 starts it there, 1 ends it there), and `nudge`
# moves the anchor off the dot, in percentage points. The nudge is multiplied
# by cwr_gap(), which cwr_figure() sets to `phone_gap` while it draws the phone
# version, where a percentage point is half as wide.
top_row <- plot_data |>
  filter(district == last(levels(district))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`2016`, `2021`), names_to = "year", values_to = "percent") |>
  mutate(
    hjust = if_else(year == "2016", 0, 1),
    nudge = if_else(year == "2016", 0.6, -0.6)
  )

p <- plot_data |>
  ggplot() +

  # Background reference segment spanning full x range
  geom_segment(aes(
    x = 0,
    xend = max_x,
    y = district,
    yend = district
    ),
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +

  # Dumbbell segment connecting x1 to x2
  geom_segment(aes(
    x = `2016`,
    xend = `2021`,
    y = district,
    yend = district
    ),
    color = "grey50",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +

  geom_point(aes(
    x = `2016`,
    y = district,
    color = "2016"
    ),
    shape = 19, size = 4
  ) +

  geom_point(aes(
    x = `2021`,
    y = district,
    color = "2021"
    ),
    shape = 19, size = 4
  ) +

  # The years, on the top row only, just above the line. grey30 is the colour
  # theme_cwr() gives the axis labels. cwr_label() rather than geom_text() so
  # the halo behind the letters clears the line each year sits over.
  cwr_label(
    data = top_row,
    aes(x = percent + nudge * cwr_gap(), y = district, label = year, hjust = hjust),
    vjust = 0, nudge_y = 0.1,
    colour = "grey30",
    size = label_size * 0.8, fontface = "bold"
  ) +

  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +

  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2016" = cowboysilver,
      "2021" = dodgerblue
    ),
    name = NULL,
    breaks = c("2016", "2021"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +

  # Bare numbers on the axis; the subtitle says they are percentages (rule 1c)
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max_x),
    breaks = seq(0, max_x, by = 10),
    labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", scale = 1, suffix = ""),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05)),
    position = "top"
  ) +

  # Room above the top row for the year labels
  scale_y_discrete(
    position = "left",
    labels = y_labels,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1))
  ) +

  # Horizontal chart: swap tufte's default grid orientation
  theme(
    axis.text.y.left = element_markdown(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "A year into the pandemic, the share of people working at home was still much higher than in 2016",
    subtitle = "Share^1^ of employed people who worked from home, 2016 and 2021, %",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Tables 98-10-0456-01", "98-400-X2016321"),
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        # The 2021 intervals are narrow next to the change the chart shows, so
        # they are stated rather than drawn (rule 9b); {widest} is filled from
        # the data. The 2016 table publishes none.
        str_glue(
          "95% confidence intervals for 2021 are within ±{widest} percentage points; none available for 2016",
          widest = with(
            filter(work_at_home, district != cwr_region),
            cwr_ci_widest(percent, percent_lower, percent_upper)
          )
        )
      )
    )
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, top row first
alt_lines <- plot_data |>
  arrange(desc(district)) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(
    district, ": 2016 ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(`2016`), " per cent, 2021 ",
    label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(`2021`), " per cent"
  )) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-work-at-home",
  # The year labels sit a percentage point or so off their dots, which is half
  # the distance on a phone unless it is doubled
  phone_gap = 2,
  alt = paste0(
    "Dot plot with one row per district and two dots on each row, grey for ",
    "2016 and blue for 2021, joined by a line, placed along a scale of the percentage of ",
    "employed people who worked at home. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### 2016

```{r}
#| label: work-at-home-industry
#| output: asis

# ---- Shared by both tabs of the industry chart ---------------------------

# The ten industries whose workers most often worked at home, for the Region as
# a whole: the top ten of the 20 NAICS sectors in 2016, ranked by the share of
# the sector's workers whose place of work status was "worked at home". The
# second tab adds each sector's 2021 dot, so both tabs draw the same ten rows
# in the same order and on the same scale - switching tabs adds the 2021 dot
# and the line to it, and changes nothing else. work_at_home_industry is read
# in the load-data chunk.
#
# The ggdumbbell template (the cwr-charts skill), drawn with one dot on the
# first tab and two on the second; no row is bolded, since every row is an
# industry and none of them is the focus the way the Region is on a chart of
# places.
industry_rows <- work_at_home_industry |>
  filter(year == 2016) |>
  slice_max(percent, n = 10) |>
  pull(industry)

industry_data <- work_at_home_industry |>
  filter(industry %in% industry_rows) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(industry, industry_short),
    names_from = year,
    values_from = percent
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Ordered on the 2016 share: reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal
    # chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the industry with the most
    # people working at home in 2016 ends up on top
    industry = reorder(industry, `2016`),
    # The axis draws the short form of the longest sector names, which
    # 02_clean_data.R works out; the data file keeps the published name
    y_label = industry_short,
    # How far the share moved between the censuses, for the label under each
    # dumbbell on the second tab
    change = `2021` - `2016`
  )

# Pre-compute labels to avoid data masking issue in scale_y_discrete
y_labels <- industry_data |> select(industry, y_label) |> deframe()

# The right end of the background segments and of the x axis: just past the
# largest share in either year, rounded up to the next 10, so both tabs share
# one frame
max_x <- ceiling(max(industry_data$`2021`) / 10) * 10

# The top row's dots are named with their year on the second tab, above the
# line joining them. The top row here is the one industry whose share barely
# moved between the censuses, so its two dots nearly touch: each label
# therefore sits on the outer side of its own dot - the lower value's to its
# left, the higher value's to its right - rather than facing inwards as on the
# chart of districts, where the two dots are far apart. `nudge` moves the label
# off its dot in percentage points and is multiplied by cwr_gap(), which
# cwr_figure() sets to `phone_gap` while it draws the phone version, where a
# percentage point is half as wide.
top_row <- industry_data |>
  filter(industry == last(levels(industry))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`2016`, `2021`), names_to = "year", values_to = "percent") |>
  mutate(
    hjust = if_else(percent == min(percent), 1, 0),
    nudge = if_else(percent == min(percent), -0.9, 0.9)
  )

# One chart for each tab: `with_2021` adds the second dot, the line joining it
# to the 2016 dot, and the year labels. Those layers are added as a list, which
# keeps the joining line underneath both dots.
industry_dumbbell <- function(with_2021 = FALSE) {
  ggplot(industry_data) +

    # Background reference segment spanning full x range
    geom_segment(aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = max_x,
      y = industry,
      yend = industry
      ),
      color = "grey80",
      linewidth = 0.3
    ) +

    (if (with_2021) list(
      # Dumbbell segment connecting x1 to x2
      geom_segment(aes(
        x = `2016`,
        xend = `2021`,
        y = industry,
        yend = industry
        ),
        color = "grey50",
        linewidth = 0.7
      )
    )) +

    geom_point(aes(
      x = `2016`,
      y = industry,
      color = "2016"
      ),
      shape = 19, size = 4
    ) +

    (if (with_2021) list(
      geom_point(aes(
        x = `2021`,
        y = industry,
        color = "2021"
        ),
        shape = 19, size = 4
      ),

      # The years, on the top row only, just above the line. grey30 is the
      # colour theme_cwr() gives the axis labels. cwr_label() rather than
      # geom_text() so the halo behind the letters clears the line each year
      # sits over.
      cwr_label(
        data = top_row,
        aes(x = percent + nudge * cwr_gap(), y = industry, label = year, hjust = hjust),
        vjust = 0, nudge_y = 0.1,
        colour = "grey30",
        size = label_size * 0.8, fontface = "bold"
      ),

      # How much the share moved since 2016, in percentage points, centred
      # under each dumbbell and in the 2021 colour, since it is the 2021 dot
      # that moved. Rounded to whole points: a tenth of a point is well inside
      # what the 2016 table's random rounding can shift. The nudge clears the
      # dots on the row where the two nearly touch (agriculture); a row is
      # about as deep on a phone as on a desktop, so it needs no cwr_gap().
      cwr_label(
        aes(
          x = (`2016` + `2021`) / 2,
          y = industry,
          label = label_number(accuracy = 1, style_positive = "plus")(change)
        ),
        vjust = 1, nudge_y = -0.19,
        colour = dodgerblue,
        size = label_size * 0.8, fontface = "bold"
      )
    )) +

    geom_vline(
      xintercept = 0,
      color = "black",
      linewidth = 0.5
    ) +

    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(
        "2016" = cowboysilver,
        "2021" = dodgerblue
      ),
      name = NULL,
      breaks = c("2016", "2021"),
      guide = "none"
    ) +

    # Bare numbers on the axis; the subtitle says they are percentages (rule 1c)
    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = c(0, max_x),
      breaks = seq(0, max_x, by = 10),
      labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", scale = 1, suffix = ""),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05)),
      position = "top"
    ) +

    # Room above the top row for the year labels, kept on both tabs so the rows
    # do not shift when the tab changes
    scale_y_discrete(
      position = "left",
      labels = y_labels,
      expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1))
    ) +

    # Horizontal chart: swap tufte's default grid orientation
    theme(
      axis.text.y.left = element_markdown(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      axis.line.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
    )
}

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, top row first, with the
# published sector names rather than the short forms the axis draws
industry_alt <- function(with_2021 = FALSE) {
  lines <- industry_data |>
    arrange(desc(`2016`)) |>
    mutate(line = if (with_2021) {
      paste0(industry, ": 2016 ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(`2016`),
             " per cent, 2021 ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(`2021`), " per cent")
    } else {
      paste0(industry, " ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(`2016`), " per cent")
    }) |>
    pull(line)

  paste0(
    if (with_2021) {
      paste0(
        "Dot plot with one row per industry and two dots on each row, grey for ",
        "2016 and blue for 2021, joined by a line, placed along a scale of the ",
        "percentage of the industry's workers in Waterloo Region who worked at home. "
      )
    } else {
      paste0(
        "Dot plot with one row per industry and one grey dot on each row, placed ",
        "along a scale of the percentage of the industry's workers in Waterloo ",
        "Region who worked at home in 2016. "
      )
    },
    paste(lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  )
}

# ---- This tab ------------------------------------------------------------
p <- industry_dumbbell() +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-pandemic, farmers were by far the most likely to work at home",
    subtitle = "Waterloo Region, share of workers who worked at home, by industry^1^, 2016, %^2^",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-400-X2016321",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Top 10 industries only",
        # The 2016 tables publish no interval for any count, so none can be
        # worked out for these shares (rule 9b)
        "No confidence intervals are published for these figures; shares close together may differ only by sampling error"
      )
    )
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-work-at-home-industry",
  alt = industry_alt()
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

p <- industry_dumbbell(with_2021 = TRUE) +

    subtitle = "Waterloo Region, share of workers who worked at home, by industry^1^, %^2^ and percentage point change",
    caption = cwr_caption(

        str_glue(
          "95% confidence intervals for 2021 are within ±{widest} percentage points; none available for 2016",
          widest = with(
            filter(work_at_home_industry, year == 2021, industry %in% industry_rows),

  # The year labels sit a percentage point or so off their dots, which is half

  alt = industry_alt(with_2021 = TRUE)

:::

```{r}
#| label: commuting
#| output: asis

# A stacked bar rather than a lollipop, because these three numbers are parts of
# one whole - every worker who lives in the municipality is in exactly one of
# them - and a stack shows a share of the row at a glance where three separate
# dots would not.
commuting_bars <- commuting |>
  mutate(
    # Drawn in order of distance from home, nearest first, so every bar reads
    # left to right as "how far do people go".
    destination = factor(
      destination,
      levels = c("In their own district", "Elsewhere in the Region", "Outside the Region")
    ),
    # Ordered on the share who stay put. fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a
    # horizontal chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the municipality
    # whose workers are most self-contained ends up on top.
    district = fct_reorder(
      district,
      if_else(destination == "In their own district", percent, 0),
      .fun = max
    ),
    label = label_number(accuracy = 1, suffix = "%")(percent),
    # A segment narrower than about a tenth of the bar cannot hold a two-digit
    # percentage, so those go unlabelled rather than overhanging into their
    # neighbour. Read off a render; nothing here is that narrow yet, but the
    # numbers move when the census does.
    label = if_else(percent >= 10, label, "")
  )

destination_colours <- c(
  `In their own district` = dodgerblue,
  `Elsewhere in the Region` = dodgerblue50,
  `Outside the Region` = cowboysilver
)

p <- ggplot(commuting_bars, aes(x = percent, y = district, fill = destination)) +
  # reverse = TRUE stacks the first level at the left. Left to itself ggplot2
  # stacks factor levels from the right, which would put the longest journey
  # nearest the axis and read backwards.
  geom_col(width = 0.7, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  # position_stack() with vjust 0.5 puts each label in the middle of its own
  # segment rather than at the end of the bar.
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE),
    colour = "white", size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The segments are named on the bars rather than in a legend: nearest above
  # the top bar at its start, furthest above it at its end, and the one in
  # between under the bottom bar. cwr_stack_keys() in R/theme_cwr.R places
  # them from the data, and draws the baseline.
  cwr_stack_keys(
    commuting_bars, percent, district, destination,
    labels = c(
      `In their own district` = "HOME DISTRICT",
      `Elsewhere in the Region` = "ELSEWHERE IN REGION",
      `Outside the Region` = "OUTSIDE REGION"
    ),
    colours = destination_colours
  ) +
  # Dark to light as the distance grows: the eye reads the ramp as distance
  # without being told. The colours mean distance here, not city and township,
  # so the bars carry their own key.
  scale_fill_manual(values = destination_colours, guide = "none") +
  # The bars fill the width by construction, so the axis says nothing the
  # segments do not.
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  # Room above the top bar and below the bottom one for the segment names. On a
  # discrete scale `add` is in rows, and cwr_figure() counts it into the height.
  # cwr_short_name() gives the house short form of a long municipal name.
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(1.1, 0.9)), labels = cwr_short_name) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Where each district's commuters work",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0462-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Includes only workers with a fixed place of work outside the home.",
        # The intervals are narrow next to the gaps the chart shows, so they
        # are stated rather than drawn (rule 9b). The sentence is yours to
        # edit; {widest} is filled with the widest interval on the chart,
        # measured from the data by cwr_ci_widest().
        str_glue(
          "95% confidence intervals are within ±{widest} percentage points",
          widest = with(commuting_bars, cwr_ci_widest(percent, percent_lower, percent_upper))
        )
      )
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

alt_lines <- commuting_bars |>
  mutate(entry = paste0(destination, " ", label_number(accuracy = 1)(percent), " per cent")) |>
  summarise(entries = paste(entry, collapse = ", "), .by = district) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(district, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-commuting",
  alt = paste0(
    "One horizontal bar per district, each split into three parts: the ",
    "share of its workers who work in their own district, the share who ",
    "work elsewhere in Waterloo Region, and the share who work outside it. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

```{r}
#| label: commuting-mode
#| output: asis

# How people get to work, one panel per mode. Each panel has its own x scale,
# so the transit and active bars stretch to fill their panels and the
# differences between places are visible, rather than being dwarfed by the car
# bars. The cost is that bar lengths cannot be compared across panels; the
# labels carry that. (A shared scale - drop scales = "free_x" - keeps it.)
commuting_mode <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "commuting_mode.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

# Roughly how many characters of label fit across one panel of a three-panel
# chart at this font size. Read off a render.
panel_chars_three <- 28

mode_bars <- commuting_mode |>
  mutate(
    # The panel headings, in Statistics Canada's wording and in the order the
    # panels are drawn. "Active transportation" carries the key to note 2. Panel
    # headings are plain text, not ggtext, so <sup>2</sup> would print as
    # written; the Unicode superscript character is used instead.
    mode = factor(
      mode,
      levels = c("Car, truck or van", "Public transit", "Active transportation"),
      labels = c("Car, truck or van", "Public transit", "Active transportation²")
    ),
    # One order for all three panels, set on the first, so a place sits on the
    # same row in each and can be read straight across. fct_reorder() sorts
    # ascending and the first level is drawn at the bottom, so the most
    # car-dependent municipality ends up on top.
    district = fct_reorder(
      district,
      if_else(mode == "Car, truck or van", percent, 0),
      .fun = max
    ),
    # One decimal place: the transit and active shares are small enough that
    # whole numbers would round several of them to the same value, or to 0.
    # A share is missing where 02_clean_data.R blanked it: its sampling error
    # is so large that Statistics Canada's scale rates it E ("use with
    # caution") or F ("too unreliable"), and this site uses neither. The row
    # stays, named "Not reported" with the key to note 3, rather than drawn as a
    # zero. geom_text() draws plain text, so the key is the Unicode
    # superscript, not <sup>. (Wellesley's transit share is a true zero: no
    # sampled household reported it, and it is charted as published.)
    label = if_else(
      is.na(percent),
      "Not reported³",
      label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent)
    )
  ) |>
  # Whether a label fits inside its bar, asked panel by panel because each
  # panel has its own scale: the longest bar in the panel sets it, and the axis
  # runs to about 1.2 times that.
  mutate(
    inside = !is.na(percent) &
      percent >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(percent, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.2 / panel_chars_three),
    .by = mode
  )

p <- ggplot(mode_bars, aes(x = percent, y = district)) +
  # One colour for every bar: the panels already say which mode is which, and
  # the cities and townships are not being compared here.
  geom_col(data = mode_bars |> filter(!is.na(percent)), width = 0.7, fill = dodgerblue) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      # A missing share's text starts at the baseline, in grey
      x = coalesce(percent, 0),
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it - hjust flips the text about its
      # anchor, and the anchor is the end of the bar either way
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      colour = case_when(inside ~ "white", is.na(percent) ~ "grey30", .default = "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  # Room on the right for any label that sits outside its bar
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  # The house short form of a long municipal name
  scale_y_discrete(labels = cwr_short_name) +
  facet_wrap(vars(mode), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  # Stops a label that overhangs the panel edge from being cut off
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "How commuters get to work, by district",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0464-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Other ways of getting to work are not shown, so the three do not add to 100%",
        "Active transportation is walking or cycling",
        # Keyed ³ on each share not reported; drops out on its own if none is
        if (any(is.na(pull(mode_bars, percent)))) {
          "The sampling error exceeds 16.6%, so the value is too unreliable to report."
        },
        # Who is counted, from the census dictionary's "Main mode of commuting".
        # Unlike the first chart, this one also counts people with no fixed
        # workplace address. Last in the list so the keys above keep their
        # numbers.
        "Includes workers with a usual place of work or no fixed workplace address."
      )
    )
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed. Each line reads down its panel
# in the order the rows are drawn, top first.
alt_lines <- mode_bars |>
  arrange(mode, desc(district)) |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = mode
  ) |>
  # The superscript keys mean nothing read aloud, so the panel's is dropped and
  # a missing share's reason is said in words
  mutate(line = paste0(
    str_remove(mode, "²"), ": ",
    str_replace_all(entries, "Not reported³", "not reported, sampling error too large")
  )) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-commuting-mode",
  alt = paste0(
    "Three panels of blue horizontal bars, each on its own scale, one row per ",
    "district, showing the share of commuters who travel to work by car, ",
    "truck or van, by public transit, and by active transportation (walking ",
    "or cycling). ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
  # Three panels side by side will not fit across a phone, so the phone version
  # stacks them. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(mode), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x"))
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### Kitchener

```{r}
#| label: flows-kitchener
#| output: asis

# Where each municipality's workers go, one map per tab. Every tab draws the
# same map from a different home municipality: each municipality shaded by the
# share of the home municipality's workers who work there, labelled with its
# name and that share, and a red arrow to the most common workplace outside the
# Region. The map is built once here by flow_map() and each tab adds its own
# titles.
library(sf)

# Every commute from a Region municipality, one row per home and place of work
flows <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "commuting_flows.csv"),
  col_types = cols(home_csd = col_character(), work_csd = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  # The City of Brantford and the County of Brant that wraps around it are two
  # census subdivisions but one place as far as a commute is concerned, so they
  # are counted together, as the feeder chart further down does. Matched on
  # their codes, because "Brant" alone would also catch Brantford. The pair
  # keep Brant's code, whose point in flow_places.csv marks them on the map.
  mutate(
    brant_pair = work_csd %in% c("3529005", "3529006"),
    work = if_else(brant_pair, "Brantford/Brant", work),
    work_csd = if_else(brant_pair, "3529005", work_csd)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    workers = sum(workers), percent = sum(percent),
    .by = c(home_csd, home, work_csd, work, in_region)
  ) |>
  # So the most common workplace outside the Region is picked again. It is the
  # same place for every municipality as before; for North Dumfries, Brant
  # becomes Brantford/Brant and its share grows.
  mutate(
    top_outside = !in_region & workers == max(workers[!in_region]),
    .by = home_csd
  )

# The Region's seven outlines, projected into the house map projection
# (cwr_map_crs, in R/maps.R). Everything drawn on the map is projected the same
# way, so coordinates are metres east and north and every distance below is in
# metres.
region_shapes <- st_read(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "region_shapes.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  st_transform(cwr_map_crs)

# The middle of every place the map marks: the seven municipalities, where
# their labels go, and the three places outside the Region that are someone's
# top destination. Projected like the shapes and turned into plain x and y
# columns, so the arrows can be worked out with ordinary arithmetic.
map_points <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "flow_places.csv"),
  col_types = cols(csd = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(cwr_map_crs) |>
  (\(points) bind_cols(
    st_drop_geometry(points),
    st_coordinates(points) |> as_tibble() |> set_names(c("x", "y"))
  ))()

label_points <- map_points |> filter(in_region)
outside_places <- map_points |>
  filter(!in_region) |>
  # Named as the combined place above, so its label is measured at the width it
  # is drawn
  mutate(name = if_else(csd == "3529005", "Brantford/Brant", name))

# The outside places are drawn closer than they are. Brant's middle is 20 km
# beyond the Region's edge and Stratford's 17, and a frame wide enough to show
# them at their true distance leaves the Region itself small on the page - small
# enough that the labels inside Waterloo and Cambridge no longer fit. So each is
# pulled in towards the middle of the Region until it sits no more than 5 km
# beyond the edge: in the right direction, at a shortened distance, which the
# caption says. (Setting `outside_reach` to Inf puts them back.)
outside_reach <- 5000
region_outline <- st_union(region_shapes)
region_middle <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(region_outline))
outside_places <- outside_places |>
  mutate(
    beyond = as.numeric(st_distance(
      st_as_sf(outside_places, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = cwr_map_crs),
      region_outline
    )),
    pull_in = pmax(beyond - outside_reach, 0),
    reach = sqrt((x - region_middle[1])^2 + (y - region_middle[2])^2),
    x = x - pull_in * (x - region_middle[1]) / reach,
    y = y - pull_in * (y - region_middle[2]) / reach
  ) |>
  select(-beyond, -pull_in, -reach)

share_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")

# ---- How big the labels are -------------------------------------------------
# Every label has to sit comfortably inside its municipality on both versions
# of the chart, so its size on the map has to be known in metres. That takes
# two numbers: how big the text is on the page, and how many metres of map a
# millimetre of page covers.
#
# The first is measured, by asking grid (the drawing system underneath ggplot2)
# how wide and tall the text comes out in Inter. The measurement needs a
# graphics device to be open, so one is opened on a throwaway file and closed
# again - after which R is pointed back at whatever device it was using, since
# closing one moves R on to the next rather than the one before.
label_font_mm <- label_size * 0.9   # geom_text() sizes are in millimetres
text_size_mm <- function(labels, bold = TRUE) {
  previous <- dev.cur()
  ragg::agg_png(tempfile(fileext = ".png"))
  sizes <- map(labels, \(text) {
    grob <- grid::textGrob(text, gp = grid::gpar(
      fontfamily = cwr_font(), fontsize = label_font_mm * .pt,
      fontface = if (bold) 2 else 1, lineheight = 0.95
    ))
    tibble(
      w_mm = grid::convertWidth(grid::grobWidth(grob), "mm", valueOnly = TRUE),
      h_mm = grid::convertHeight(grid::grobHeight(grob), "mm", valueOnly = TRUE)
    )
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
  dev.off()
  if (previous > 1) dev.set(previous)
  sizes
}

# The second follows from the frame. The desktop chart is 8.3 inches wide and
# `flow_height` tall; the phone chart 4.2 inches wide. On a phone the map fills
# the width, so a millimetre is the frame's width over the 101 mm the panel
# gets. On a desktop the map is limited by its height instead: the panel gets
# what is left after the title, subtitle and notes, about 2.1 inches of them.
# Phone labels are drawn at `flow_phone_text_scale` of their desktop size (the
# house default is 0.8; a little smaller here, because Waterloo and Cambridge
# are narrow).
flow_height <- 7.5
flow_phone_height <- 6
flow_phone_text_scale <- 0.72
phone_panel_mm <- 4.2 * 25.4 - 5.6
desktop_panel_mm <- c(w = 8.3 * 25.4 - 4.2, h = (flow_height - 2.1) * 25.4)

# Each outside place is labelled above its dot if it lies north of the Region's
# middle and below it if south, so the label widens the frame by only half its
# width. The frame is the Region plus those dots and labels, with a margin, and
# it is the same on every tab so switching tabs never moves the map. The label
# sizes depend on the frame and the frame on the label sizes, so the two are
# worked out twice; the second pass changes nothing visible.
outside_text <- text_size_mm(paste0(outside_places$name, "\n00.0%"))
outside_places <- bind_cols(outside_places, outside_text) |>
  mutate(above = y > region_middle[2])
# Far enough that an arrowhead arriving level with the dot stays clear of it
label_gap <- 1400
frame_margin <- 1000
region_box <- st_bbox(region_shapes)
frame_for <- function(metres_per_text_mm) {
  boxes <- outside_places |>
    mutate(
      w = w_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
      h = h_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
      xmin = x - w / 2, xmax = x + w / 2,
      ymin = if_else(above, y + label_gap, y - label_gap - h),
      ymax = if_else(above, y + label_gap + h, y - label_gap)
    )
  x <- range(region_box[c("xmin", "xmax")], boxes$xmin, boxes$xmax) + c(-frame_margin, frame_margin)
  y <- range(region_box[c("ymin", "ymax")], boxes$ymin, boxes$ymax) + c(-frame_margin, frame_margin)
  list(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    # Metres of map per millimetre of text on each version, allowing for the
    # text's own shrinking on the phone; labels are sized for the larger
    metres_per_text_mm = max(
      diff(x) / phone_panel_mm * flow_phone_text_scale,
      diff(x) / desktop_panel_mm[["w"]],
      diff(y) / desktop_panel_mm[["h"]]
    )
  )
}
# A first guess of 400 m, then once more from the frame that guess gives
frame <- frame_for(frame_for(400)$metres_per_text_mm)
frame_x <- frame$x
frame_y <- frame$y
metres_per_text_mm <- frame$metres_per_text_mm

# ---- Where the labels go ------------------------------------------------------
# Each municipality's label - its name over its share - goes where the whole
# two-line label has the most room inside its borders, found by
# cwr_label_spot() in R/maps.R. That is not the same as the middle of the
# shape: on this map, with three places outside the Region to make room for,
# "Waterloo" over its figure is about as wide as Waterloo itself, so the label
# sits where the widest gap between borders can hold it. Labels are never
# tilted, and the same spot is used on every tab.
#
# The two lines are measured separately and handed to cwr_label_spot() as two
# widths: "Waterloo" is half as wide again as "15.8%", and treating the label
# as one block as wide as the name keeps it higher in a shape that narrows
# downwards than it needs to be.
#
# Names are measured as they are drawn, in the house short form (cwr_short_name()
# turns "North Dumfries" into "N. Dumfries").
name_size <- text_size_mm(cwr_short_name(region_shapes$name))
share_size <- text_size_mm(rep("00.0%", nrow(region_shapes)))
label_spots <- region_shapes |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  bind_cols(text_size_mm(paste0(cwr_short_name(region_shapes$name), "\n00.0%"))) |>
  mutate(
    w = w_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
    h = h_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
    name_w = name_size$w_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
    share_w = share_size$w_mm * metres_per_text_mm,
    spot = pmap(
      list(st_geometry(region_shapes), name_w, share_w, h),
      \(shape, name_w, share_w, h) {
        cwr_label_spot(st_sfc(shape, crs = cwr_map_crs), c(name_w, share_w), h)
      }
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(spot)

# A label's box, used only to keep the arrow below clear of the words
box_polygon <- function(x, y, w, h) {
  corners <- rbind(c(-w, -h), c(w, -h), c(w, h), c(-w, h), c(-w, -h)) / 2
  st_polygon(list(sweep(corners, 2, c(x, y), "+")))
}

# ---- The arrow out of the Region ---------------------------------------------
# A gently bowed arrow from the home municipality's label to the outside place,
# as a run of points: a quadratic Bezier curve from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1),
# pulled towards a control point set off to the left of the straight line by
# `bend` times its length (negative bends go right). It starts where it leaves
# the home label's box, which is padded by 600 m so the line starts clear of
# the text, and stops 1.5 km short of the dot, clear of the dot's label.
bowed_arrow <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, bend, start_box) {
  cx <- (x0 + x1) / 2 - bend * (y1 - y0)
  cy <- (y0 + y1) / 2 + bend * (x1 - x0)
  t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 120)
  points <- tibble(
    x = (1 - t)^2 * x0 + 2 * (1 - t) * t * cx + t^2 * x1,
    y = (1 - t)^2 * y0 + 2 * (1 - t) * t * cy + t^2 * y1
  )
  in_start_box <- st_within(
    st_as_sf(points, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = cwr_map_crs), start_box, sparse = FALSE
  )[, 1]
  points |>
    filter(!in_start_box, sqrt((x - x1)^2 + (y - y1)^2) >= 1500)
}

# Of five bends, the arrow takes the one that passes furthest from the other
# labels - the other municipalities' and the outside place's own - so it does
# not run through a name.
outside_arrow <- function(home_name, destination) {
  home_spot <- label_spots |> filter(name == home_name)
  label_box <- function(spot, room) {
    st_sfc(box_polygon(spot$x, spot$y, spot$w + 2 * room, spot$h + 2 * room), crs = cwr_map_crs)
  }
  others <- label_spots |>
    filter(name != home_name) |>
    (\(spots) map(seq_len(nrow(spots)), \(i) label_box(spots[i, ], 0)))() |>
    reduce(c) |>
    c(destination_label_box(destination)) |>
    st_union()
  map(c(0.2, 0.1, 0, -0.1, -0.2), \(bend) {
    path <- bowed_arrow(home_spot$x, home_spot$y, destination$x, destination$y, bend,
                        label_box(home_spot, 600))
    line <- st_sfc(st_linestring(as.matrix(path)), crs = cwr_map_crs)
    list(path = path, clearance = as.numeric(st_distance(line, others)))
  }) |>
    (\(options) options[[which.max(map_dbl(options, "clearance"))]]$path)()
}

# The outside place's label box, where flow_map() draws it: centred over or
# under the dot, `label_gap` away
destination_label_box <- function(destination) {
  w <- destination$w_mm * metres_per_text_mm
  h <- destination$h_mm * metres_per_text_mm
  y_middle <- if (destination$above) destination$y + label_gap + h / 2 else destination$y - label_gap - h / 2
  st_sfc(box_polygon(destination$x, y_middle, w, h), crs = cwr_map_crs)
}

# ---- The map ------------------------------------------------------------------
# One shading scale for every tab, so the same blue means the same share
# wherever it appears. 60% is just above the largest share, Cambridge's
# workers who work in Cambridge.
fill_low <- "#EEF3F8"
fill_limits <- c(0, 60)

# Label text is white on the darker fills and black on the lighter ones;
# cwr_text_on_fill() reads the fill's own lightness to decide.

flow_map <- function(home_name) {
  shares <- region_shapes |>
    left_join(
      flows |> filter(home == home_name) |> select(csd = work_csd, percent),
      join_by(csd)
    ) |>
    # A municipality nobody from the home one works in has no row: 0%
    mutate(percent = replace_na(percent, 0))

  labels <- label_spots |>
    left_join(st_drop_geometry(shares) |> select(csd, percent), join_by(csd)) |>
    mutate(
      is_home = name == home_name,
      text_colour = cwr_text_on_fill(percent, fill_low, dodgerblue, fill_limits)
    )

  destination <- flows |>
    filter(home == home_name, top_outside) |>
    left_join(outside_places |> select(work_csd = csd, x, y, above, w_mm, h_mm), join_by(work_csd))

  ggplot() +
    # White borders between shaded shapes separate neighbours without drawing
    # a second thing to look at
    geom_sf(data = shares, aes(fill = percent), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = fill_low, high = dodgerblue, limits = fill_limits, guide = "none") +
    # The red arrow first, so the labels are drawn over it if it ever grazes one
    geom_path(
      data = outside_arrow(home_name, destination),
      aes(x, y),
      colour = habsred, linewidth = 0.9,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "in"), type = "closed", angle = 25),
      lineend = "butt", linejoin = "mitre"
    ) +
    geom_point(data = destination, aes(x, y), colour = habsred, size = 2) +
    geom_text(
      data = destination,
      aes(x, y, label = paste0(work, "\n", share_label(percent)),
          vjust = if_else(above, 0, 1)),
      nudge_y = if_else(destination$above, label_gap, -label_gap),
      colour = habsred, fontface = "bold", size = label_font_mm, lineheight = 0.95
    ) +
    # The municipality's name, bold for the home one, over its share
    geom_text(
      data = labels,
      aes(x, y, label = paste0(cwr_short_name(name), "\n", share_label(percent)),
          colour = text_colour),
      fontface = if_else(labels$is_home, "bold", "plain"),
      size = label_font_mm, lineheight = 0.95
    ) +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    # The same frame on every tab. datum = NA drops the latitude and longitude
    # grid.
    coord_sf(xlim = frame_x, ylim = frame_y, expand = FALSE, datum = NA) +
    cwr_map_theme()
}

flow_caption <- function(home_name) {
  cwr_caption(
    c("Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0459-01", "the 2021 census boundary files"),
    credit = TRUE,
    notes = c(
      "Share of workers with a usual place of work",
      paste0("The share on ", cwr_short_name(home_name), " is of people who both live and work there"),
      "Red marks the most common workplace outside the Region, in its direction but nearer than it is"
    )
  )
}

# Alt text built from the same numbers the map draws
flow_alt <- function(home_name) {
  shares <- region_shapes |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    left_join(
      flows |> filter(home == home_name) |> select(csd = work_csd, percent),
      join_by(csd)
    ) |>
    mutate(percent = replace_na(percent, 0))
  stay <- shares |> filter(name == home_name)
  elsewhere <- shares |> filter(name != home_name) |> arrange(desc(percent))
  outside <- flows |> filter(home == home_name, top_outside)
  paste0(
    "Map of Waterloo Region's seven districts, each shaded darker the ",
    "larger the share of ", home_name, "'s workers who work there. ",
    share_label(stay$percent), " of ", home_name, "'s workers work in ",
    home_name, ". Elsewhere in the Region: ",
    paste(paste(elsewhere$name, share_label(elsewhere$percent)), collapse = ", "),
    ". A red arrow points to the most common workplace outside the Region, ",
    outside$work, ", with ", share_label(outside$percent), "."
  )
}

p <- flow_map("Kitchener") +
  labs(
    title = "Where commuters from Kitchener work",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = flow_caption("Kitchener")
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-flows-kitchener",
  alt = flow_alt("Kitchener"),
  height = flow_height, phone_height = flow_phone_height,
  phone_text_scale = flow_phone_text_scale
)
```

```{r}
#| label: destinations
#| output: asis

# Where the Region's cross-municipality commuters end up. The denominator is
# every commute that crosses a municipal border inside the Region: people who
# work in the municipality they live in are left out, because the question is
# where commuters go, and so are people who leave the Region, because the seven
# shares are meant to add to 100. `flows` is read in the first tab above.
between <- flows |>
  filter(in_region, home != work) |>
  summarise(workers = sum(workers), .by = work) |>
  rename(district = work)

# Roughly how many characters fit across the panel at this font size, read off
# a render; it decides whether a bar is long enough to hold its own label.
panel_chars <- 40

# Both this chart and the one below rank the seven municipalities the same way:
# a plain bar for each one's share, labelled. Shares, not numbers of people:
# commuting is asked on the census long-form questionnaire, which goes to one
# household in four, so a count here is an estimate scaled up from a sample
# rather than a headcount. A share of the same sample is what it measures well.
# The chart is built once here and each chunk adds its own titles. `ranked`
# needs a district and a count; the share is worked out from the counts, which
# is what makes the bars add to 100.
rank_chart <- function(ranked) {
  ranked <- ranked |>
    mutate(
      percent = workers / sum(workers) * 100,
      district = fct_reorder(district, percent),
      share_label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent),
      # Whether a bar can hold its own label
      inside = percent >= (nchar(share_label) + 1.5) * (max(percent) * 1.05 / panel_chars)
    )

  ggplot(ranked, aes(x = percent, y = district)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7, fill = dodgerblue) +
    # The baseline the bars grow from, stopping just past the end bars
    annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = nrow(ranked) + 0.5,
             colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
    # White inside a bar that can hold its label, black just past one that cannot
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = share_label,
        hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
        colour = if_else(inside, "white", "black")
      ),
      size = label_size * 0.8
    ) +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    # Room on the right for a label that sits outside its bar
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
    # The house short form of a long municipal name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = cwr_short_name) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      axis.line.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
    )
}

# The rows of an alt text, read top to bottom in the order the bars are drawn
rank_lines <- function(ranked) {
  ranked |>
    mutate(percent = workers / sum(workers) * 100) |>
    arrange(desc(percent)) |>
    mutate(line = paste0(district, " ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent))) |>
    pull(line)
}

p <- rank_chart(between) +
  labs(
    title = "Commuters from elsewhere in the Region, by the district they work in",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0459-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Workers with a usual place of work",
        "Only commutes that cross a municipal border inside the Region are counted",
        "No confidence intervals are published for these figures; shares close together may differ only by sampling error"
      )
    )
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-destinations",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars ranking the seven districts by their share of the ",
    "Region's commuters who travel to work in another district in the ",
    "Region. ",
    paste(rank_lines(between), collapse = ". "), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### Where they work

```{r}
#| label: inbound-districts
#| output: asis

# The commuters the charts above leave out: people who live outside the Region
# and work in it. One row per place they live in and municipality they work in.
inbound <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "commuting", "data", "commuting_inbound.csv"),
  col_types = cols(home_csd = col_character(), work_csd = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

# This tab: which municipality they work in. rank_chart() is the bar chart
# built above, so the two look the same and are read the same way.
inbound_districts <- inbound |>
  summarise(workers = sum(workers), .by = work) |>
  rename(district = work)

p <- rank_chart(inbound_districts) +
  labs(
    title = "Commuters from outside the Region, by the district they work in",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0459-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Workers with a usual place of work",
        "Only commutes into the Region from a home outside it are counted"
      )
    )
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-inbound-districts",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars ranking the seven districts by their share of the ",
    "people who commute into Waterloo Region from outside it. ",
    paste(rank_lines(inbound_districts), collapse = ". "), "."
  )
)
```

### Where they come from

```{r}
#| label: inbound-feeders
#| output: asis

# This tab: the ten municipalities that send the most commuters into the
# Region, as each one's share of everyone who commutes in - a share, not a
# count, for the same long-form sampling reason as the bars above. The share
# is taken before the top ten are picked, so its denominator is every inbound
# commuter, not just these ten. A lollipop rather than bars, because the ten values are close
# together in the middle of the ranking and a thin segment with a dot at its
# end is easier to compare there than ten filled bars.
feeders <- inbound |>
  # The City of Brantford and the County of Brant that wraps around it are two
  # census subdivisions but one place as far as a commute is concerned, so they
  # are counted together. Matched on their codes, because "Brant" alone would
  # also catch Brantford.
  mutate(home = if_else(home_csd %in% c("3529005", "3529006"), "Brantford/Brant", home)) |>
  summarise(workers = sum(workers), .by = home) |>
  mutate(percent = workers / sum(workers) * 100) |>
  slice_max(percent, n = 10) |>
  mutate(home = fct_reorder(home, percent))

p <- ggplot(feeders, aes(x = percent, y = home)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = percent, y = home, yend = home),
               colour = cowboysilver, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(shape = 19, size = 3.5, colour = dodgerblue) +
  # The baseline the segments grow from, stopping just past the end rows
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = nrow(feeders) + 0.5,
           colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # The dots carry no numbers, so the chart keeps an axis. It goes on top, as
  # every ranked horizontal chart here does: a reader meets the scale before
  # the rows rather than after them. Bare numbers, no % on every break: the
  # subtitle says they are percentages, which is where a unit of measure is
  # always reported.
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 15, by = 5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    position = "top"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "The ten places sending the most commuters into the Region",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0459-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Workers with a usual place of work",
        "The ten places sending the most commuters into the Region",
        "No confidence intervals are published for these figures; shares close together may differ only by sampling error"
      )
    )
  ) +
  # A horizontal chart reads against vertical gridlines, so the theme's
  # horizontal ones are swapped for them
  theme(
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-inbound-feeders",
  alt = paste0(
    "A lollipop chart of the ten places that send the most commuters ",
    "into Waterloo Region, ranked by each one's share of everyone who commutes ",
    "in, against an axis along the top in percent. ",
    paste(
      feeders |>
        arrange(desc(percent)) |>
        mutate(line = paste0(home, " ", label_number(accuracy = 0.1, suffix = "%")(percent))) |>
        pull(line),
      collapse = ". "
    ), "."
  )
)
```
